title: Unconscious Bias

slides.title: One DSD People, Access and Culture
slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Unconscious Bias

Examining how assumptions influence DSD services, workplace opportunities, and the routines that connect them.

Self-directed Foundation learning for all staff
slides.narration:
A first impression can feel like knowledge before we have examined what supports it. This course gives you room to notice that moment and consider what could follow from it. Our practice examples connect service contact, policy decisions, and community participation with recruitment, onboarding, supervision, development, and retention.

You can work independently, make a choice in each case, and read the explanation before continuing. Keep two questions nearby: What does the evidence establish, and what could this response make easier or harder for the person? Those questions help you examine both a decision and a routine that may repeat it.

slides.title: First impressions
slides.text:
First impressions

A familiar colleague and a newer employee offer service proposals. The newer employee brings community feedback the team has not heard.

Which proposal would you first trust? Before continuing, name the evidence that could change your view.

If familiarity settles the choice, a useful concern may never reach the decision.
slides.narration:
Picture yourself receiving these two proposals. You know how the familiar colleague works, so their explanation may feel easier to trust. That feeling does not tell you which proposal responds more effectively to the service question.

Pause before moving on. What would you compare: the evidence, the practical options, or the people heard? The newer employee’s feedback could reveal a barrier the team’s usual account misses. If the familiar proposal is accepted without examining that concern, the barrier may remain. Give each proposal a comparable chance to explain its contribution, then choose on relevant evidence rather than familiarity alone.

slides.title: What a picture cannot tell us
slides.text:
What a picture cannot tell us

Appearance, accent, disability, and communication style do not establish competence, motivation, or priorities.

A quick impression can affect how much explanation a person receives or whose work gets considered.

Separate what you observe from what you infer. What evidence does this decision need?
slides.narration:
An image or short introduction tells us something, but usually less than our first reaction suggests. We might fill the gaps with a familiar story about age, accent, disability, or appearance. That story can then influence a decision.

In services, someone may receive less explanation because staff assume they will not understand. In recruitment, relevant experience may be overlooked because the applicant does not resemble the usual candidate. Neither impression is enough. Ask what the role or conversation requires and which evidence would establish it. A culture brief can prepare questions; it cannot supply this person’s abilities, preferences, or motives.

slides.title: Learning focus
slides.text:
Learning focus

Notice where an assumption enters a service, policy, or workforce decision.

Test the evidence and compare what different responses could cause.

Trace how repeated contact, selection, or development routines can make a barrier persist. Identify what remains unknown.
slides.narration:
You will practice moving from an impression to a decision and then to its possible effect. An unsupported service description might discourage the next contact. An informal development invitation might keep another employee from gaining experience used in a later selection.

That sequence helps explain why bias matters beyond a single thought. We still need evidence about what happened, who had access, and which explanations fit. In each case, identify a reasonable response and the information it would help you obtain. You do not have to identify someone’s hidden beliefs to examine whether a routine creates an avoidable barrier.

slides.title: Practice: a missed service contact
slides.text:
Practice: a missed service contact

Two service calls went unanswered. A record says the person “does not care.” What response would avoid turning that assumption into a service barrier?

A. Check contact conditions and preferred communication before drawing a conclusion about motivation.

B. Treat the existing label as confirmation that more contact is pointless.

C. Use a culture brief to infer why this person did not respond.

In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Check contact conditions and preferred communication before drawing a conclusion about motivation.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Treat the existing label as confirmation that more contact is pointless.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Use a culture brief to infer why this person did not respond.

slides.narration:
Think about the choice before selecting an answer. What do the unanswered calls establish? What did the words “does not care” add? You are choosing both a next response and a way of carrying information into the next decision.

Consider the possible consequences. One response keeps inquiry open; another may stop contact; a third may replace the person’s account with group assumptions. Choose the most careful response, then read how it could affect access. These are examples for practice circumstances, so there is no need to identify a person or share a case.

slides.title: Why this response helps
slides.text:
Why this response helps

The unanswered calls are known; the reason is not. Checking timing, language, and method may reveal a barrier staff can address. Recording those facts can prevent an unsupported label from shaping later contacts. Ask what communication works for the person, then review whether follow-up offers a usable chance to respond.

How could this label affect the person’s access during later contacts?

Continue learning

Take a moment with this question: How could this label affect the person’s access during later contacts? You can reconsider your response before continuing. Keep your attention on the actual practice and the evidence you would need.

slides.title: Another way to consider this
slides.text:
Another way to consider this

Treating the label as proof could end follow-up before the person has a usable chance to respond. Repeated in later contacts, this assumption could become a reason to withhold explanation or support. Examine the contact conditions and what happened; unanswered calls alone do not establish indifference.

Another way to consider this

A brief can prepare questions, but using it to explain an individual can hide the actual contact barrier or personal choice. Repeating that shortcut may carry group assumptions into later service decisions. Ask about communication and examine the evidence; the reason for no response remains unknown.

slides.title: Learning at your own pace
slides.text:
Learning at your own pace

Use the practice situations to examine your reasoning privately.

You do not need to disclose personal experiences, test results, or case information.

You can reconsider an answer after reading the feedback. Focus on the decision, its possible effects, and the evidence still needed.
slides.narration:
Learning about bias can bring discomfort, questions, or recognition. You can take the time you need and work with the practice situations without sharing anything personal. An initial answer is a place to begin thinking, not a judgment about your character.

The explanations may point to an overlooked perspective or a possible barrier. Consider whether that reasoning changes your view. You may also notice a different question that would improve the decision. The purpose is to understand the subject and make judgments you can explain and revise. No colleague or community member needs to provide a personal story for your learning to be meaningful.

slides.title: Understanding unconscious bias
slides.text:
Understanding unconscious bias

Unconscious bias involves associations or assumptions that can influence interpretation without deliberate awareness.

“Implicit bias” often describes related concepts. An association, a decision, and a disparity provide different evidence.

Examine how an impression may shape a decision and its effects; one does not automatically prove the other.
slides.narration:
Unconscious bias can influence which explanation feels likely, whose knowledge feels credible, or what we notice first. A person may sincerely value fairness and still need to examine a judgment. Unconscious and implicit bias overlap in everyday use, although research may define them more precisely.

An association is not the same as a decision, and an outcome difference does not reveal private beliefs. Follow the actual choice: Which information mattered? Was the criterion relevant? What could the choice prevent or make possible? Those questions connect the concept with something we can examine without diagnosing another person.

slides.title: Reflection: a routine decision
slides.text:
Reflection: a routine decision

A referral calls a person “difficult to contact.” The next staff member considers ending follow-up.

What information would you check before accepting that description?

Compare the possible effects of stopping contact and trying a usable alternative. What still needs to be learned?
slides.narration:
Pause with this referral. We know someone wrote the description, but not which contact attempts were made or what prevented a response. The number could be wrong; the message could be unclear; or the person may have decided not to respond.

Think through two facts you would check. Then consider the next decision’s effect. Ending follow-up could leave the person without a usable chance to ask about services. A suitable alternative could make that chance available, but does not guarantee a response. Careful inquiry preserves the person’s choice while avoiding a barrier created by an untested interpretation.

slides.title: Research and everyday practice
slides.text:
Research and everyday practice

Research findings depend on the setting, people studied, and what was measured.

Awareness of bias, decision quality, and service or workplace outcomes are different questions.

Use research to identify a mechanism worth examining. Check the actual decision and local evidence before claiming a pattern.
slides.narration:
Research can help you recognize a question worth asking, such as whether familiarity influences judgments under uncertainty. Ask who was studied, what was measured, and how closely the setting resembles the situation you are examining.

A study does not establish that a particular DSD decision was biased. It may suggest information to collect or a comparison to make. If a revised invitation appears to widen participation, you would still ask who received it, what support was available, and what else changed. Keep awareness, a new practice, and an improved outcome distinct. The explanation becomes stronger when it matches the evidence.

slides.title: Bias in human-services work
slides.text:
Bias in human-services work

Assumptions can shape whose concern is heard, what a service record says, and which policy option receives attention.

Listening only to familiar partners may leave an access barrier unexplored.

Ask whose experience is missing, how their input could affect the choice, and what the evidence supports.
slides.narration:
Imagine that a team’s usual partners find a service explanation clear. People unable to use the contact route never reached those partners and are absent from the discussion. Accepting the familiar feedback as the full picture could leave that access barrier unchanged.

Engagement can reveal missing experience when people have a usable chance to contribute while choices remain open. A culture brief prepares better questions; it does not replace listening. Look for what feedback changes in the analysis, not just how much was collected. Leave room for evidence that supports the original approach as well. Careful inquiry can strengthen a proposal or revise it.

slides.title: Practice: evidence in a policy proposal
slides.text:
Practice: evidence in a policy proposal

A polished service proposal hears only from the team’s usual partners. People facing access barriers are missing. What response would best test the proposal before those barriers are carried forward?

A. Treat clear writing as evidence that the proposal is ready.

B. Apply the relevant criteria, examine missing perspectives, and seek evidence that could challenge the proposal.

C. Reject the proposal because familiar partners contributed.

In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Treat clear writing as evidence that the proposal is ready.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Apply the relevant criteria, examine missing perspectives, and seek evidence that could challenge the proposal.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Reject the proposal because familiar partners contributed.

slides.narration:
The proposal may be useful and well presented. The question is whether its evidence is complete enough to support the choice. People unable to use the usual service route may also be missing from familiar partners’ feedback.

Before choosing, imagine each response’s effect. Would it leave an access barrier unexplored, discard useful knowledge, or make the decision more open to evidence? Select a response and read the explanation, then consider what the proposal would need to show.

slides.title: Another way to consider this
slides.text:
Another way to consider this

Clear writing does not establish service access. Approving successive proposals on that basis could preserve an unusable contact route or missing explanation. Examine the purpose, evidence, and likely effects, then seek perspectives that are missing. The proposal may have strengths, but its appearance cannot resolve the access question.

How would you check whether missing perspectives changed the proposal?

Try another response

slides.title: Why this response helps
slides.text:
Why this response helps

Relevant criteria and challenging evidence help test the proposal. Hearing from people affected may reveal a missing barrier; doing this across successive proposals can prevent familiar voices from becoming the only source of knowledge. Compare or revise options using what you learn. Participation itself does not establish that the service will work.

slides.title: Another way to consider this
slides.text:
Another way to consider this

Rejecting familiar partners could remove useful evidence. The concern is the incomplete account. Excluding either familiar or less-heard voices repeatedly can narrow what later proposals address. Examine what each contribution establishes and seek missing perspectives before comparing options; familiarity alone does not settle the proposal’s quality.

slides.title: Bias and declared beliefs
slides.text:
Bias and declared beliefs

An automatic association may differ from a person’s stated values.

Under pressure, a familiar explanation can receive less scrutiny and shape a consequential choice.

Examine criteria, information, and effects. A useful correction does not depend on proving someone intended harm.
slides.narration:
We can care about fairness and still rely on a familiar explanation when time is short. A supervisor may offer an opportunity to the colleague who comes to mind first. A service team may use its usual contact method without checking whether people can use it.

The concern becomes practical when that shortcut affects access. Who did not hear about the opportunity? What happened after contact failed? We do not need to decide whether someone meant harm before improving a poorly supported choice. We do need to understand the facts, preserve appropriate responsibilities, and check whether the response addresses the barrier identified.

slides.title: Affinity bias
slides.text:
Affinity bias

Affinity bias favors people who feel familiar or similar.

Informal invitations may keep recruitment, mentoring, and development within the same circle.

If the pattern repeats, people outside that circle may lack the experience later called “readiness.” How could access be widened?
slides.narration:
Affinity can make a relationship feel comfortable and a choice feel obvious. The familiar colleague may be capable; the question is whether familiarity is doing more work than relevant evidence. Someone outside the circle may be capable too, without knowing how to express interest.

Follow that possibility through employment. Missing early assignments may lead to less visible experience, less sponsorship, and fewer routes to advancement. This is a plausible mechanism, not a finding about every difference. Examine invitations, criteria, support, and participation. Community partnerships deserve similar care when the same organizations are invited and other useful knowledge never enters the conversation.

slides.title: Confirmation bias
slides.text:
Confirmation bias

Confirmation bias favors information that supports an existing belief.

A label such as “uncooperative” can make a missed call seem decisive and other explanations easy to overlook.

If the label follows the person, later decisions may repeat the barrier. What evidence could challenge it?
slides.narration:
Once a person is called uncooperative, a missed call can seem like confirmation. A returned call or an account of an inaccessible message may receive less attention because it does not fit the expected story.

The effect can travel with the record. Another staff member may shorten an explanation or stop trying an alternative. The resulting difficulty may then appear to confirm the label. Check whether that sequence actually occurred rather than assuming it did. A useful record names the event, known conditions, and open question. In performance reviews, the same discipline keeps an early impression from deciding how every later contribution is interpreted.

slides.title: The halo effect
slides.text:
The halo effect

The halo effect lets one favorable impression influence judgments about unrelated qualities.

A polished proposal can seem effective before its evidence, feasibility, and access effects are examined.

If presentation replaces scrutiny, an existing barrier may survive the proposed change. Assess each relevant quality separately.
slides.narration:
A polished presentation can make a complex proposal easier to follow. It does not establish that the proposal works or reaches the people concerned. The halo effect appears when that impression spreads into judgments needing their own evidence.

Consider a service proposal whose clear graphics hide an English-only response step. Approving it because it looks complete could preserve the access barrier in a more attractive form. Ask how the response route works and whose experience informed it. In recruitment or advancement, confidence needs the same distinction from capability. Appreciate the communication while assessing each quality the decision actually requires.

slides.title: Perception bias
slides.text:
Perception bias

Perception bias occurs when assumptions about a group shape how behavior is understood.

Quietness may be mistaken for disengagement, or an accent for limited expertise.

If those impressions govern invitations and feedback, a contribution can remain unseen. What evidence would give a fuller account?
slides.narration:
A quiet colleague may be considering the question or contributing through written analysis. Quietness alone cannot establish disengagement. An unfamiliar accent does not establish limited expertise either.

Think about what follows if that interpretation governs the next choice. The colleague may miss a visible assignment, leaving less evidence of the contribution they could make. In a service conversation, staff may speak to a companion and miss the person’s priorities. Ask what the task needs and how the person can contribute. Briefs can introduce context, but the individual’s explanation and relevant evidence are essential. A person’s identity does not settle their preferences or capacity.

slides.title: Practice: development and advancement
slides.text:
Practice: development and advancement

A supervisor offers legislative-analysis assignments to familiar employees, then cites that experience in advancement decisions. What response would help examine and improve this opportunity route?

A. Keep invitations informal because experienced employees are easier to select.

B. Ask employees to disclose personal bias-test results.

C. Clarify opportunities and relevant criteria, then examine who can participate and gain experience.

In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Keep invitations informal because experienced employees are easier to select.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Ask employees to disclose personal bias-test results.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Clarify opportunities and relevant criteria, then examine who can participate and gain experience.

slides.narration:
This case follows an opportunity across several decisions. The invitation creates experience, and that experience is later used to justify advancement. The sequence may explain a barrier, but evidence about access, criteria, support, and participation is still needed.

Consider what each response changes. Would it keep the same circle in place, require private information unrelated to access, or help employees reach a relevant opportunity? Make your choice, read the explanation, and follow the possible effects into later feedback and development.

slides.title: Another way to consider this
slides.text:
Another way to consider this

Informal invitations can keep experience inside the same circle. When that experience later becomes the readiness criterion, others may lose both the assignment and a route to advancement. Compare how people heard about the work, the criteria, and support before concluding why participation differed.

How could this opportunity route affect advancement and retention?

Try another response

Continue learning
slides.narration:
Selecting experienced employees can meet an immediate need. The question is how employees gained that experience and whether others had a usable route to acquire it. Repeating the informal invitation can keep the next opportunity dependent on the last.

Examine invitations, capabilities, support, and later judgments; differences might have several causes. Return to the choice and consider a response that makes those conditions visible instead of assuming the familiar route is the only workable one.

slides.title: Another way to consider this
slides.text:
Another way to consider this

Personal test results do not establish whether employees could reach this opportunity. Requiring disclosure could add a barrier while leaving the invitation routine unchanged. Examine actual access, criteria, support, and participation; a test cannot substitute for evidence about these decisions.

How could this opportunity route affect advancement and retention?

Try another response

Continue learning
slides.narration:
A bias-test result cannot tell you whether an employee saw the invitation, could participate, or received useful support. Requiring disclosure could turn a learning measure into an employment gate while leaving the actual process untouched.

Keep the inquiry close to the decision: who heard about the assignment, which criteria were used, and what happened afterward? Return to the case and consider which response would provide evidence without requiring private test information.

slides.title: Why this response helps
slides.text:
Why this response helps

Clear invitations and relevant criteria give employees a better chance to express interest and demonstrate capability. Support may also be needed to make participation usable. Follow the route into recognition and later decisions, checking what changed; the invitation alone does not establish equitable advancement.

How could this opportunity route affect advancement and retention?

Continue learning
slides.narration:
You chose to clarify access and criteria. That helps distinguish relevant capability from familiarity and identify support needed for participation. It does not promise an assignment, promotion, or a particular result.

Follow the route over time. Onboarding may reveal who knew how to express interest; mentoring affects preparation; workload can limit participation; feedback influences whose contribution is recognized. Comparing those conditions helps identify a barrier that a clearer invitation alone might not remove.

slides.title: A decision process we can examine
slides.text:
A decision process we can examine

A team offers development assignments through informal recommendations.

Examine who learns about the work, the criteria used, and the support available to participate.

Early access can shape experience, recognition, advancement, and retention. Trace that sequence before claiming what caused an unequal result.
slides.narration:
Look beyond the final choice for an assignment. Was the opportunity visible during onboarding? Could someone learn the skill through mentoring? Was support available, and was the work recognized later? Several stages of employment can connect.

Repeated informal invitations may create a cycle in which the same people gain the experience that justifies the next invitation. Compare actual opportunities, criteria, support, and participation over time; differences may have more than one explanation. A clearer invitation is promising when access is the issue, but follow-up should establish whether people could use it. It does not guarantee advancement or fair outcomes.

slides.title: Practice: observation or assumption?
slides.text:
Practice: observation or assumption?

“Two calls were not returned” records an event. “The person does not care” adds an unsupported claim about motivation.

Rewrite the second note using only what is known. Leave the reason for no response open.

Consider how each version could affect the next staff member’s contact decision.
slides.narration:
Try rewriting the note before continuing. A careful version might say which calls were made, whether a message was left, and what response is known. It would not need to describe motivation without relevant evidence.

Imagine reading your revised note before the next contact. Does it help identify a useful question or alternative? The unsupported version could discourage inquiry; the careful version keeps it possible. Records often influence people who did not witness the original event. A factual account does not remove every barrier, but avoids creating one through an assumption. It also supports clearer supervisory feedback and an employee’s opportunity to respond.

slides.title: Practice: fair criteria
slides.text:
Practice: fair criteria

A supervisor calls the employee who speaks most in meetings “the most engaged.”

Name two contributions the role actually needs, then consider the evidence for each employee.

When visibility becomes the standard, written analysis or careful follow-through may lose credit and development opportunities.
slides.narration:
Take a moment to identify what engagement should mean for this role. Speaking may matter, but so might sound analysis, a useful written question, follow-through, or relevant community feedback.

Rewarding only the most visible behavior can overlook contributions and affect later development or promotion discussions. That does not mean every quiet employee contributes effectively; the work evidence matters. Compare the same relevant expectations across employees and explain the judgment. Community engagement skills can count when they fit the role. An employee should not be expected to provide those skills or represent a community solely because of identity.

slides.title: Practices that reduce avoidable bias
slides.text:
Practices that reduce avoidable bias

Separate observations from interpretations. Look for evidence that could change the first explanation.

Define relevant criteria before comparing people or proposals, and hear perspectives that test the preferred answer.

Return to the effects: did the revised contact, invitation, or explanation reduce the barrier, and what remains uncertain?
slides.narration:
Useful habits give you something specific to examine. You can revise an unsupported note, clarify a criterion, ask about a contact method, or make an opportunity easier to find. Each response should fit the concern rather than serve as a general declaration of fairness.

Recruitment, onboarding, supervision, development, retention, and departure can reveal different parts of a process. Service feedback and engagement can do the same for a public-facing routine. Ask what improved after a revision and what stayed difficult. Other conditions may also explain the result. Follow-up keeps you open to improving the response instead of assuming that a well-intended change settled the issue.

slides.title: Continuing the learning
slides.text:
Continuing the learning

Choose a service or workforce decision, or a suitable example within your responsibility.

Identify the impression, the decision it could shape, and the barrier or opportunity that might follow. Name the missing evidence.

Use One DSD community briefs, engagement resources, and the Equity Analysis Toolkit to deepen the inquiry.
slides.narration:
Continue with one manageable question: a service contact, a policy proposal, or a development invitation. Trace the connection between the assumption, the choice, and the possible effect. Identify which evidence and perspectives would help you understand it.

If the concern repeats, the Equity Analysis Toolkit can help examine the surrounding process. Briefs can prepare questions, and engagement can bring in experience you have not heard. You do not need to turn private reflection into an assignment or share personal information. The aim is a clearer understanding of bias and a response that improves access or judgment within the responsibilities you actually hold.

audience: All staff, including supervisors and managers
outcomes: Explain automatic associations, first impressions, and decision shortcuts without treating them as a complete account of behavior.
Separate an observation from a judgment about motivation, credibility, or ability.
Use relevant evidence and transparent criteria to interrupt an assumption.
Identify how repeated individual shortcuts can become a routine that distributes opportunity or burden unevenly.
